Yet research on climate\u2010policy participation has focused largely on formal participation opportunities, paying less attention to citizens' expectations regarding governance roles and their evaluations of policy processes. This study examines how three survey\u2010derived governance role orientations\u2014governmental, civic, and industry\u2010and\u2010media orientations\u2014and perceived climate policy governance quality are associated with two participation outcomes: institutional participation intention and climate\u2010related civic participation behavior. The analysis uses data from a nationwide quota\u2010based online survey of 500 adults in South Korea and applies hierarchical regression models. Civic orientation is positively associated with both participation outcomes, whereas governmental orientation is negatively associated with institutional participation intention. Industry\u2010and\u2010media orientation is not significantly associated with either outcome. Perceived climate policy governance quality is positively associated with both institutional participation intention and civic participation behavior, but none of its interactions with the three orientations is statistically significant. The findings distinguish citizens' expectations about governance roles from their evaluations of governance\u2010process quality. They suggest that civic orientation and favorable process evaluations operate as separate and largely additive correlates of climate\u2010policy participation. Effective participation strategies should therefore combine meaningful institutional openness with durable connections to citizen\u2010 and civil society\u2010led climate
